qs.q: A 66-year-old man has a friction rub on chest auscultation, BUN of 100 mg/dL, and creatinine of 9.8 mg/dL. Most likely form of pericarditis?
qs.e: Severe uremia from renal failure triggers fibrin exudation onto pericardial surfaces, producing fibrinous pericarditis with a classic friction rub on auscultation.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Pericarditis is inflammation of the pericardial sac that causes chest pain, friction rub, and ECG changes. It can be acute, subacute, or chronic, and may progress to tamponade or constriction.

sections.p: Pericarditis is diagnosed by a combination of clinical features, ECG, echocardiography, and inflammatory markers. Classic ECG shows diffuse ST elevation and PR depression.
b: Chest pain, often sharp and pleuritic

t.b: Detects diffuse ST elevation and PR depression; absence suggests alternative diagnosis
Shows pericardial effusion, tamponade physiology, or thickened pericardium
Elevated levels support inflammatory process; normal may occur in early disease

sections.p: Severity is staged by clinical presentation and imaging. Stage 1: acute, uncomplicated. Stage 2: effusive or tamponade. Stage 3: constrictive.

t.b: Assesses effusion size and hemodynamic impact; large effusion with diastolic collapse indicates tamponade

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, infections dominate. Viral (e.g., enterovirus) is most common, followed by bacterial (TB, HIV), rheumatic fever, and post‑MI.
b: Bacterial (tuberculosis, HIV), especially in endemic areas

t.b: Screen for TB pericarditis; positive suggests TB etiology

sections.p: Patients report sharp, pleuritic chest pain that improves when sitting up. A friction rub may be heard, and dyspnea can occur if effusion is large.
b: Pain worse on lying flat, better upright

sections.p: Investigations confirm diagnosis, assess severity, and identify cause. Prioritize tests that are available locally.

t.b: Detects diffuse ST elevation and PR depression; absence suggests alternative diagnosis
Shows effusion size, tamponade physiology, or thickened pericardium
Elevated levels support inflammatory process; normal may occur in early disease

sections.p: Urgent complications include cardiac tamponade, constrictive pericarditis, and sudden death. Red flags are dyspnea, hypotension, pulsus paradoxus, and muffled heart sounds.

t.b: Excessive drop in systolic BP on inspiration indicates tamponade

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first. NSAIDs or colchicine reduce inflammation; steroids are reserved for refractory or autoimmune cases. Drainage is required for tamponade.

t.b: Reduce inflammation and pain; avoid in renal failure or bleeding risk
Prevents recurrence; avoid in severe renal impairment
Use only if infection excluded; high risk of infection

sections.p: Patients should be monitored for recurrence and progression to constriction. Prevention focuses on treating infections early and managing rheumatic fever.
Conditions that mimic pericarditis include myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism, pleurisy, and pneumothorax.

t.b: Elevated in MI but normal in pericarditis

sections.p: Low‑grade fever and normal CRP can occur in early viral pericarditis. Small effusions may be missed on transthoracic echo.
b: Early viral pericarditis may have normal CRP

t.b: Small effusions may be missed; consider repeat imaging if clinical suspicion remains

faq.a: Yes, most acute cases are viral, especially in young adults.

faq.q: Is a pericardial rub always present?
faq.a: Not always; it is heard in about 50% of cases and may be absent in large effusions.
Only if NSAIDs and colchicine fail and an autoimmune cause is suspected; infection must be ruled out.
